coherence.reasons: Both run a clean line from governing thought to slides. X's chain is tighter: the prize is small, the flat fee draws heavy users, Pro with a pool protects margin, mobile is the larger and compounding lever, so sequence mobile first, with pilot gates tied to the low case and explicit triggers for Q2. Its one loose joint is staffing: it assumes the 14 engineers are free in Q3–Q4 without delaying mobile, flagged only as 'CTO to confirm'. Y's four-part structure is also consistent, but it has internal tensions. It calls the mobile delay 'the real cost' and then asks to 'keep the mobile rewrite team and date fixed' while diverting 14 engineers. Its headline of $2.9M rests on the high-case precedent that it elsewhere calls untested. Its 'net $2.4M' sets benefits at their ceiling against a cost at its ceiling.

judgment.reasons: Both reach defensible conclusions under the key: Y fits R1 (Pro tier with cap, Q2, delay accepted explicitly) and X fits R1 packaging with R3 sequencing, meeting R3's conditions by quantifying the win-rate risk (at most $0.6M) and planning a paid random pilot as the interim AI response. X weighs the central trade-off better. It costs the delay in both directions ($0.5–1.1M permanent churn against at most $0.6M at risk plus deferred contribution), admits it is a close call, and separates permanent churn from deferred revenue. It names two triggers that would flip the answer to Q2 and tests more options (free in Core, add-on, Pro with and without a pool). Y accepts the delay on a net-ARR sum that uses 33% uptake and the full win-back ceiling on the benefit side. It does not consider that mobile churn compounds or that Pro is a one-time NRR step, and its only safeguard is to 'lock the new date'. Y's conditions and two-quarter review are sensible but thinner.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key calculations correctly: $8.1M against $2.45M, inference of $32/$61/$131 per month, 109 deals worth $0.64M, Pro at $2.89M, and the 74.1% no-cap stress. Both flag the volunteer bias, the survey's 6% response and size skew, and the Routewise discount, and both dismantle the VP Sales claim. X goes further and its extra figures check out: low and high cases, a 9–22% sampling range on the paywall rate, add-on margins of 59% and 12%, contribution and payback, company margin under five scenarios, the 64% adoption break-even, and churn ARR by reason ($2.2M against $0.5M). It also notes that Routewise's AI launched only in the last month of Q3. Y adds two good points: loss notes cover all lost deals, and the 26% threshold for the NRR gap. But Y plans on a single $2.9M figure from a precedent for a non-AI tier with no downside case. Its slide 5 title leans causal on the win-rate fall, though caveated. Its 'both risks at their ceiling' net figure also puts the benefits at their ceiling. X's weak spot is the assumption that mobile is unaffected by Q3–Q4 Copilot engineering.

revision.reasons: Both revise the CPO hypothesis as the key expects: they keep 'launch', reject the $8M survey sizing in favour of the paywall test, and replace the flat $149 add-on with a per-seat Pro tier with a usage allowance because adopters are heavy users. Both also reject the VP Sales inference. X revises more fully. It treats 14% as a ceiling and plans on a range of $1.2–2.9M, states that the add-on is not a fallback, and takes the Head of Customer Success's mobile concern seriously enough to change the sequencing while keeping an explicit route back to Q2. Y replaces the $8M with a single $2.9M plan figure that rests on the 2023 precedent, which is a milder correction of the optimism, and keeps the Q2 timing with less scrutiny.

overall.reasons: Both documents avoid every major trap and land on defensible recommendations with correct core numbers. X would serve the CEO better. It gives ranges instead of point estimates, a two-sided costing of the delay, and the point that Pro is a one-time NRR step while a mobile fix recurs. It stress-tests margin, sets pilot gates with thresholds, and names triggers for reverting to a Q2 launch. Its main weakness is the unverified assumption that deferring Copilot removes the mobile conflict. Y is concise and correct, and its Q2 launch is a legitimate call, but its case for accepting the mobile delay rests on a best-case net-ARR sum and gives less protection if uptake falls short.
